case.case_title: Subbash Chandra Fernando v. Kapilaratne, Officer-in-Charge, Police Station, Gampaha and Others
case.source_citation: Sri Lanka Law Reports [1992] 1 Sri L.R. 305

clause.text: Any person detained shall be brought before a judge and cannot be held without legal order.

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the petitioner’s detention under Emergency Regulations and preventive detention order violated Article 13(2) due to excessiveness and lack of legal justification.
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioner claimed unlawful and excessive detention after termination of criminal proceedings, violating Article 13(2).
case_context.respondent_argument: The Secretary of Defence had valid subjective satisfaction to order preventive detention; detention was reviewed periodically and justified by conduct.
key_facts: Petitioner was detained under Emergency Regulations and a preventive detention order from 20.07.89 to at least 02.01.91.
Criminal proceedings against petitioner ended with admission of offences and payment of costs.
Advisory Committee recommended release but it was not acted upon.
Petitioner alleged detention was excessive and not necessary to prevent threat to national security or public order.
Court considered evidence of conduct, material relied on by Secretary, and duration of detention.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: Article 13(2) requires detention to be lawful and not excessive; preventive detention orders must be based on reasonable probability of threat and are subject to court review for reasonableness.
reasoning.application_to_facts: The court found the initial detention order valid based on subjective satisfaction and material considered by the Secretary; however, prolonged detention beyond 02.01.91 was excessive and unlawful.
principles_established: Preventive detention orders must be based on subjective satisfaction of reasonable probability of threat.
Courts can review such orders applying a test of reasonableness in a wide sense.
Excessive detention beyond necessity violates Article 13(2).
precedents_cited: Breen v. Amalgamated Engineering Union (1971) QB175
Wickremabandu v. Cyril Herath SC Application No. 27/88

outcome.holding: The initial detention order was valid, but detention after 02.01.91 was excessive and violated Article 13(2); petitioner was ordered released and awarded compensation.
outcome.remedy_or_orders: Release of petitioner from custody and payment of Rs. 9000 compensation plus Rs. 1500 costs.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 13(2) was central to the court’s finding that prolonged detention without necessity was unlawful, leading to release and compensation.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: The court held that the detention order was valid initially but the prolonged detention after 02.01.91 was excessive and invalid, directing release and compensation.
